Innocent III. Reigning from 1198 to 1216, Innocent III represents the absolute zenith of medieval papal authority and influence. He was the first pope to systematically assert the title Vicar of Christ as his primary claim to absolute authority. Claiming supreme sovereignty over both church and state, he acted as the ultimate arbiter of European politics, frequently deposing kings and commanding empires.

In 1215, he convened the Fourth Lateran Council, which defined the doctrine of transubstantiation, mandated annual confession and communion for all Catholics, and required Jews and Muslims to wear distinguishing dress. In 1208, he placed England under an interdict and subsequently excommunicated King John over a dispute regarding the appointment of Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury, eventually forcing John to surrender England as a papal vassal. Innocent formulated the sun and moon allegory in his letter Sicut universitatis conditor, asserting that papal authority, the sun, is inherently superior to royal power, the moon, which only derives its light from the papacy. In 1215, at King John's request, he declared the Magna Carta null and void, issuing a papal bull that released the king from his oath under threat of excommunication.

Innocent intervened in the succession of the Holy Roman Empire, switching support between Otto IV and Frederick II, whom he successfully installed as emperor after securing Frederick's vow to protect papal lands. In 1202, he initiated the Fourth Crusade, which was diverted by Venetian interests and ended in the brutal sack of Constantinople in 1204, establishing the Latin Empire and deeply alienating the Eastern Orthodox Church. In 1209, he launched the Albigensian Crusade to eradicate the Cathar heresy in southern France, representing the first crusade directed against heretics within Christian Europe.

Innocent verbally approved the Franciscan Order after a famous dream in which he saw Francis of Assisi holding up the collapsing basilica of St. John Lateran. He confirmed the founding of the Dominican Order led by Dominic of Caleruega, mobilizing their academic and preaching skills to counter heresy.
